reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight is that spatial perception arises from the ability to distinguish localized sensory effects. When a stimulus excites only part of a sensory surface, the brain interprets this as evidence of a discrete external cause. This leads to a dualism between internal sensation and external causality. The capacity for partial stimulation is necessary for such discrimination. In olfaction and gustation, full-surface activation yields a unified, undivided sensation—hence, spatial extension is not perceived. In contrast, sharp stimuli like alum or pepper excite localized regions, enabling precise spatial localization. This principle extends to audition where high notes appear as thin streaks against a background, indicating localized auditory processing. The failure mode occurs when uniform excitation prevents any spatial inference, resulting in a holistic, undifferentiated perceptual field.
